prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The authors argue, convincingly, that existing formulations are either closed-world, require explicit specification of unseen attribute types at inference time, or rely on noisier distant supervision. In contrast, the proposed setting asks the model to both expand known seed attribute types and discover entirely new attribute types automatically. This is a meaningful step toward realistic e-commerce information extraction. The paper also contributes a new dataset, WoaM, and a method, Amacer, that combines seed-supervised contrastive learning with two forms of weak implicit supervision derived from product context. Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and stronger on problem formulation and empirical engineering than on methodological novelty in the strictest sense. My assessment is positive, though there are several important concerns around evaluation design, dataset scope, and the exact strength of the claims.

The main strengths of the paper are clear. First, the task formulation is valuable. The distinction between zero-shot extraction of named unseen attributes and automatic discovery of previously unspecified attributes is important, and the paper articulates this gap well. Second, the dataset construction appears thoughtful. The hybrid seed-set creation process—automatic sanitization followed by lightweight human curation—is a sensible compromise between scalability and quality, and is arguably one of the most practically useful contributions here. Third, the method is coherent and well aligned with the task constraints. The pipeline of candidate generation, embedding refinement, adaptive expansion for seed attributes, and clustering for residual candidates is intuitive. The use of self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence and latent-attribute regularization is also a reasonable attempt to inject signal for unseen attributes, where direct supervision is absent. Fourth, the empirical gains over the chosen baselines are substantial, especially relative to OA-Mine variants, and the ablations suggest that each component contributes.

I also appreciate that the paper does not oversell complete success on new attribute discovery. The qualitative analysis is honest in showing that many unseen attributes are either missed or absorbed into existing seed clusters. This transparency improves the credibility of the work. The decomposition by seed versus new types and title versus bullet points is also useful and helps clarify where the gains come from.

That said, I have several substantive concerns.

The biggest issue is evaluation. The paper frames the task as open-world attribute mining, where outputs are clusters corresponding to attribute types, including previously unnamed ones. However, the main scalar metric is a “pseudo-F1” constructed by averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different statistical behavior; averaging them and treating the result as “precision” is not theoretically justified. Because the paper’s central claims hinge on improvements of this pseudo-F1, the validity and robustness of the conclusions depend heavily on this metric choice. The authors do report the underlying metrics separately, which helps, but the headline result would be much stronger if supported by more standard evaluation protocols for open extraction and clustering. At minimum, the paper should better justify why this aggregation is meaningful, and ideally include alternative summaries such as pairwise precision/recall/F1 over clustered spans, B-cubed metrics, or cluster-level matching metrics.

Relatedly, the evaluation conflates two subproblems: span extraction and attribute grouping. The paper does provide a separate span extraction analysis in Table 5 and a “gold spans as candidates” analysis in Table 4, which is good, but the main narrative still centers on end-to-end pseudo-F1. Since candidate generation is a major source of performance variation, it would be helpful to more systematically disentangle extraction quality from clustering quality. For example, reporting clustering performance conditioned on correctly extracted spans, or reporting cluster purity/completeness on matched spans only, would make the gains easier to attribute.

A second concern is the limited dataset scope. WoaM contains only four product categories, all from Amazon, all in English, and all with around 9k products each. This is a reasonable starting point, but the paper makes fairly broad claims about practical open-world attribute mining. It is not yet clear how well the approach generalizes across more diverse categories, noisier marketplaces, multilingual settings, or domains where POS tagging is less reliable. The syntax-based candidate generation is likely category- and language-sensitive, even if the POS patterns are learned automatically. The paper acknowledges dependence on POS tagging, but the broader generalization issue deserves more emphasis. In its current form, the dataset is useful, but still somewhat narrow for a benchmark intended to define a new task setting.

A third concern is that some of the empirical comparisons may not be fully balanced. The paper compares segmentation-based OA-Mine variants against syntax-based Amacer variants, and indeed shows that syntax-based candidate generation is better. But this means part of the gain comes from a different candidate generation regime rather than from the representation learning or clustering method alone. The authors do attempt to control for this with OA-Mine* and Amacer-R, which is good, but I still found the comparison landscape a bit difficult to parse. In particular, because candidate generation is so influential, stronger baselines for this stage would be valuable. For example, noun-phrase chunking, constituency-based phrase extraction, dependency-based span proposals, or modern sequence labeling with weak supervision could provide more informative comparisons than only segmentation and POS-pattern matching. The current DBSCAN and OA-Mine baselines may understate how competitive simpler alternatives could be.

A fourth issue is the novelty level of the method. The overall system is sensible, but many components are adaptations of existing ideas: supervised contrastive learning on seed values, a heuristic self-supervised co-occurrence loss, adaptive thresholding against seed supports, and a neural topic-model-style latent variable regularizer. The contribution lies more in combining these pieces for this task than in introducing a fundamentally new learning principle. That is acceptable for an applied conference paper if the empirical case is strong, but the paper occasionally uses language like “novel formulation” somewhat broadly. I would encourage the authors to calibrate the novelty claims more carefully and emphasize the integrated task-method-dataset contribution.

There are also some methodological details that need clarification. The supervised contrastive loss as written appears to use the denominator over negatives only, rather than all non-anchor examples including positives as in standard supervised contrastive formulations; if intentional, this should be discussed. The adaptive expansion threshold is based on average pairwise cosine distance within the seed set, scaled by delta. Since cosine distance and cosine similarity are both mentioned in nearby equations, the notation is potentially confusing and should be made precise. It is also unclear how sensitive performance is to the number of latent attributes K, the DBSCAN hyperparameters, and the seed-set size. Given that the paper’s premise is light supervision, a seed-budget sensitivity analysis would be especially valuable. How does performance degrade when the number of seed values per type is reduced from 22 to, say, 5 or 10? Similarly, how robust is the method to noisier seeds before human curation? These are central practical questions.

The latent attribute module is interesting, but I am not fully convinced by the evidence that it learns attribute-like structure rather than broader topical or lexical co-occurrence patterns. The qualitative examples in Table 7 are mixed: some columns clearly correspond to attributes or product facets, while others look more like product types or general concepts. Since the paper’s claim is that these latent attributes provide supervision useful for new attribute discovery, it would help to quantify this more directly. For instance, one could measure whether spans assigned high probability under the same latent attribute are more likely to share a gold attribute type than random or than simple co-occurrence baselines. Without such analysis, the mechanism remains plausible but somewhat under-validated.

The candidate generation stage is practical and appears effective, but it also seems to impose a fairly strong inductive bias on what counts as an attribute value: namely, spans matching POS patterns observed in product profiles. This may work well for many nominal/adjectival attributes, but could miss values expressed in more compositional or clause-like forms, especially in bullet points. The paper notes that exact span extraction remains weak, which is consistent with this concern. I would have liked more recall-oriented analysis of candidate generation itself: what fraction of gold spans are covered before clustering, broken down by category and by seed/new type? The “Gold” upper bound in Table 4 is helpful but indirect. Candidate coverage is a key bottleneck in this pipeline and deserves explicit reporting.

On the experimental side, the statistical significance statement is too thin. The paper says the best F1 is statistically significant by t-test at >95% confidence, but it is not clear what the sample units are. If the macro-average is over only four categories, a t-test is not very meaningful. If significance is computed over products, then dependence assumptions may be violated because clustering is global. This should be clarified or removed.

The annotation protocol also needs more detail. The paper says two in-house annotators labeled all reasonable attribute values and new types, with no overlapping spans and one type per span. But open-world attribute annotation is inherently subjective. What were the annotation guidelines for deciding whether something is a “reasonable attribute”? How were disagreements resolved? What was inter-annotator agreement on span boundaries and type assignments, especially for new types? Since the benchmark is a major contribution, annotation reliability is important.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the dataset is likely to be useful, and the method is a solid baseline-plus improvement for this new setting. The empirical gains are consistent across several comparisons, and the paper does a better-than-average job of analyzing both successes and failure modes. I especially like the practical framing around seed-set construction and the attempt to move beyond title-only extraction into richer product descriptions.

For improvement, I would strongly recommend the following. First, strengthen the evaluation section with more standard clustering and extraction metrics, and justify or de-emphasize the pseudo-F1. Second, add explicit candidate-span coverage statistics and more systematic disentanglement of extraction versus clustering. Third, provide sensitivity analyses for seed quantity/quality and latent-attribute hyperparameters. Fourth, clarify annotation quality and significance testing. Fifth, if space permits, include one or two stronger candidate-generation baselines to show that the gains are not primarily due to replacing segmentation with a better proposal mechanism.

My overall recommendation is positive but not without reservations. I view this as a worthwhile contribution mainly because it introduces a meaningful task setting and a practical benchmark, supported by a coherent method that improves over prior work. The methodological novelty is moderate, and the evaluation design needs tightening, but the paper is likely to stimulate useful follow-up work on lightly supervised open-world extraction in e-commerce.

If I were assigning a score, this would land in the weak accept to accept range.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset over four Amazon product categories with a curated seed set and human-annotated test set. The proposed method, Amacer, uses syntax-based candidate span generation via POS patterns, supervised contrastive learning on seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for remaining candidates, and two additional regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and a latent-attribute variational topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their dataset, especially in partial-match F1 and on new attribute types.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining with only light supervision and without requiring explicit descriptions of unseen target attributes.
The dataset contribution is meaningful: WoaM includes titles and bullet points, covers multiple categories, and explicitly evaluates discovery of unseen attribute types and values.
The overall pipeline is intuitive and modular, combining candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering/grouping in a way that is easy to understand and potentially reusable.
The syntax-based candidate generation is a sensible alternative to segmentation for longer bullet-point text and appears empirically stronger and more efficient than the OA-Mine segmentation setup.

The empirical gains over the strongest open-world baselines on the proposed benchmark are substantial, and the paper includes useful ablations comparing segmentation vs syntax candidates and regularized vs non-regularized variants.
The analysis distinguishes seed vs new attributes and title vs bullet-point performance, which helps clarify where the gains come from.
The paper is generally honest about limitations, especially the difficulty of new attribute discovery and topic collapse in the latent-attribute component.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is somewhat ad hoc: the main metric is a pseudo-F1 built from the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI treated as pseudo-precision, which lacks a standard theoretical justification and may distort model ranking.

The proposed method is a pipeline with many heuristic components (POS-pattern candidate generation, adaptive thresholds, DBSCAN, bullet-point heuristic, latent-topic regularization), making it difficult to isolate which parts are fundamentally responsible for gains and how robust they are across settings.
The dataset is limited to only four product categories from Amazon, so claims about general open-world product attribute mining may be broader than what the evidence supports.

The paper does not provide enough evidence about annotation quality and reproducibility of the test set, such as inter-annotator agreement, adjudication details, or ambiguity analysis for open-world attribute typing.

The comparison to baselines may not be fully balanced because some baselines are inherently disadvantaged by the new setting or by using different candidate generation assumptions; stronger modern embedding/clustering baselines are absent.

The latent-attribute module is only weakly validated: qualitative examples are shown, but there is limited quantitative evidence that the learned latent attributes correspond to coherent or distinct attribute types beyond modest end-task gains.

The method still has low span extraction precision/recall, and the paper's strongest claims about open-world discovery should be tempered given the relatively modest absolute F1 values and the qualitative failure cases.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive loss formula appears incorrect or at least nonstandard. In Eq. for L^su, the denominator sums only over N^s(i)=I^s\P^s(i), which seems to include the anchor itself and excludes positives from the normalization. Standard supervised contrastive objectives normalize over all non-anchor examples. As written, the objective is mathematically inconsistent with the cited formulation and may not match the implemented loss.

The same issue appears in the self-supervised contrastive loss L^ss: the denominator uses only negatives from different bullet points, excluding positives and likely including inconsistent candidate sets. This again deviates from standard InfoNCE/supervised contrastive formulations and weakens confidence in the mathematical specification.

The adaptive expansion thresholding uses the average pairwise cosine distance among support examples as a threshold, scaled by delta. This assumes intra-class seed dispersion is a reliable acceptance radius for unseen values, but no justification or calibration analysis is provided. Since cosine distance is smaller for more similar points, diffuse seed sets get larger thresholds and thus looser acceptance, which may amplify noisy or heterogeneous seed types.

The latent-attribute variational formulation is underspecified and partially inconsistent. Eq. (3) writes mean/variance as linear projections but does not enforce positivity of variance; likely log-variance is intended. Eq. (8) writes KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}) even though \tilde{\alpha}^p is sampled then softmaxed, while the prior is Gaussian; the KL should be between Gaussian posterior parameters and Gaussian prior before softmax, not between incompatible objects as written.

The reconstruction objective in L^un models only positive spans appearing in a product and does not describe any normalization or negative sampling beyond the softmax over batch-unique candidates. This makes the objective batch-dependent and potentially unstable, yet no sensitivity analysis is given.

The main empirical metric combines clustering scores and recall into a pseudo-F1 that is not standard and may not preserve meaningful precision-recall tradeoffs. Because Jaccard/ARI/NMI are not precision measures, interpreting their average as precision is scientifically questionable.

Statistical significance claims are weakly supported. The paper reports t-test significance over macro-averaged category scores, but with only four product categories the sample size is extremely small for reliable t-testing.

There is potential train-test resource leakage risk in candidate generation and seed construction because POS patterns are derived from product profiles and the seed set is bootstrapped from retailer-provided attributes from the same ecosystem. While not direct label leakage into the held-out test products, the setup may encode substantial schema knowledge unavailable in a truly open-world scenario; this is not carefully analyzed.
